Check the video KYC recording from onboarding, if one was done, for any visible background that indicates the actual place of work
Confirm the current settlement hold amount, the number of settlement cycles affected, and the date the hold began, since the RBI nodal account rules limit how long funds can be parked
Confirm whether any customer complaints or police or cyber-cell references exist against the merchant, as this changes the flag from a paperwork issue to a fraud issue
A written confirmation of the merchant's current principal place of business, with the complete address including building name, floor, landmark, and PIN code

A clear explanation, in writing, of why the field agent could not trace the address — for example the merchant moved, works from home, uses a co-working desk, the building is known by a different local name, or the signage is under a different trade name

A fresh officially valid address proof dated within the last two or three months, in the proprietor's name or the firm's name — electricity bill, telephone or broadband bill, gas bill, water bill, property tax receipt, or a bank statement carrying the address
If the premises are rented, a registered or notarised rent agreement or leave-and-licence agreement covering the current period, plus the latest rent receipt
If the premises are owned by the proprietor, the property ownership document or the latest property tax receipt
If the premises belong to a family member, a signed no-objection certificate from the owner along with the owner's own address proof and identity proof

If the merchant operates from a co-working space or a virtual office, the service agreement with that provider, the desk or cabin number, and a letter from the provider confirming the merchant actually occupies space there

If the business is run from home, a plain statement to that effect along with the residential address proof, since a home-based advertising service is normal and does not by itself disqualify the merchant
Geo-tagged photographs of the business premises taken recently — the building exterior, the entrance, the signboard or nameplate, and the interior work area with any staff or equipment visible
A photograph of the nameplate or signboard showing the trade name, or an explanation if no signage exists
The proprietor's PAN card copy, self-attested
The proprietor's Aadhaar or other officially valid identity document, self-attested, with the number masked as required
A recent passport-size photograph of the proprietor, if not already on file or if the one on file is unclear
The GST registration certificate if registered, showing the current principal place of business, plus the latest filed GST return
The Udyam or MSME registration certificate if the merchant holds one
The Shops and Establishments registration or trade licence issued by the local municipal authority for the current address
A professional tax registration certificate, where the state requires one
Bank account proof — a cancelled cheque bearing the proprietor's or firm's name, or a bank statement or passbook first page
The last three to six months of current account bank statements, to confirm the settlement account is live and the business cash flow is consistent with declared turnover
Where the address on the address proof differs from the address on PAN, Aadhaar, GST, or the bank record, a written reconciliation explaining each difference
A current, reachable mobile number and email address, with the merchant available for a verification call at a stated time window
Willingness to complete a video call verification, where the merchant walks the camera through the premises and reads out the building name and nearby landmarks
A detailed description of the actual business — what advertising services are sold, to whom, how clients are acquired, and how the service is delivered
Sample client contracts, work orders, or purchase orders, with at least two or three clients, showing the merchant's address as printed on the merchant's own paperwork
Sample invoices raised to clients in the last three months, again showing the business address
A client list with contact details for at least two clients willing to confirm the engagement, so the aggregator can independently verify the business exists
Evidence of service delivery — campaign reports, creative samples, published ad placements, or platform account screenshots consistent with MCC 7311
The business website or social media handles, and confirmation that the contact address published there matches the address now being declared
An explanation of any mismatch between the address published on the website or invoices and the address on file
The declared and projected monthly turnover, and an explanation if actual processing has run materially above what was declared at onboarding
A list of all operating locations if the merchant works from more than one place, marking which is the principal place of business
Details of any staff or contractors at the premises, since an advertising firm with no people and no equipment at a claimed office invites further questions
Confirmation of who has operational control of the merchant dashboard and settlement account, and whether any third party or agency operates it on the merchant's behalf
A declaration that the merchant is not acting as a front for another entity and is not permitting transaction routing for any other business
A signed undertaking that the information and documents submitted are true, with the merchant accepting liability for any false declaration
A signed undertaking to inform the aggregator in writing within a stated period of any future change of address or change in the nature of business
Written responses to any specific customer complaints or chargebacks the aggregator has on record, with supporting proof of service delivery for the disputed transactions

After documents come in, run an independent public-record check — GST portal search on the GSTIN, MCA or Udyam lookup, and a map and street-view check of the declared address — before closing the flag
Re-run the sanction, PEP, and adverse media screening on the proprietor with the updated address details
Record the final decision, the evidence relied on, and the reviewer's name in the case file, and update the master KYC record with the verified address so the same flag does not recur
Confirm whether the case meets the internal threshold for a suspicious transaction report, and route it to the principal officer if it does, independent of whether the settlement hold is released
A written request or declaration from the proprietor asking for the terminal (TID) to be reactivated, signed and dated.
A confirmation that the business is still running and still runs as a restaurant (matching MCC 5812), not a different type of business.

Proof that the business is currently open and active, such as recent purchase bills, supplier invoices, electricity bill, or recent UPI/bank statement showing business income during the dormant period.
Recent photos of the shop showing the signboard, the inside of the restaurant, and the terminal installed at the counter (with date or geo-tag if possible).
Confirmation that the business address on file is still correct, and if it has changed, the new address with proof (rent agreement, utility bill, or shop licence at the new address).
A current, valid FSSAI licence or registration (needed for a food business) if the one on file has expired.
A current shop and establishment licence, trade licence, or Udyam registration if the one on file has expired.
Confirmation that the settlement bank account on file is still active and belongs to the proprietor, with a recent cancelled cheque or bank statement if it has changed.
Re-confirmation of the proprietor's identity: current PAN and Aadhaar (or other officially valid document) if the KYC on file is old or due for periodic update.
Confirmation that the terminal device is still physically with the merchant at the registered address and has not been moved, sold, or given to anyone else.
Confirmation of expected monthly card transaction volume and average ticket size going forward, so the risk team can compare it with past behaviour.
Declaration that the merchant will not use the terminal for any other business, for cash advances, or for transactions on behalf of third parties.
GST registration details or a declaration of exemption if turnover is below the GST limit, updated if anything has changed.
The original KYC file for the proprietorship (PAN, identity proof, address proof, bank proof) to check what is on record and what has expired.
The onboarding documents showing the declared business type, MCC 5812, and the registered address, to compare with the merchant's current declarations.
The full transaction history of the TID before the dormant period, to see the normal pattern (volume, ticket size, timings) and confirm the drop to zero.

Transaction history on any other payment products the merchant uses with the aggregator (UPI QR, payment links, online gateway), to check if the business stayed active on other channels while the card terminal was idle.
Chargeback, refund, and dispute history for the account, to confirm there are no open disputes or unusual patterns before reactivating.
Any past risk flags, holds, or investigation notes on this merchant, to check for repeat issues.
Settlement and payout records, including the amount currently on hold and the bank account it is linked to.
Screening checks against negative lists: internal blacklist, card network alerts (such as MATCH/VMSS type lists), and sanctions or fraud databases, run again with current data.
A check of the merchant's name and address against public sources (website, Google listing, food delivery apps) to see signs the restaurant is still operating.
The periodic KYC review due date for this merchant, to know if a full KYC refresh is required now or only the reactivation checks.
Records of the terminal's assigned location and device serial number, to match against the photos and confirmation the merchant provides.

Field visit or agent verification reports from onboarding or any past visit; and if policy requires, an order for a fresh field visit can be raised internally (the visit itself checks the merchant, but the trigger and record are internal).
The aggregator's own dormancy policy record showing the 90-day rule, the date of deactivation, and the alert sent, to document the trigger and closure of the flag properly.
Pull the full daily transaction volume and value history for all 8 months, and mark exactly which days crossed the 7x median line and by how much.
Recompute the median itself, checking whether the baseline was set during a slow ramp-up period that makes a normal busy week look like a 7x jump.
Break the spike days down hour by hour, to see if the extra volume came in a steady business-hours flow or in sudden bursts at odd hours.
Check the average ticket size on spike days against normal days, since more customers looks very different from the same customers paying much larger amounts.
Count unique cards, unique payers and unique VPAs on the spike days, and check how many were repeat customers already seen in earlier months.
Check for card or VPA repetition patterns, such as one card used many times or a small set of cards driving most of the spike.
Look at the payment method mix on spike days (UPI, cards, netbanking, wallets) against the merchant's normal mix, and flag any sharp change.
Check which terminals, QR codes, payment links or API keys the spike traffic came through, and whether any of them were newly created or newly activated.
Review payer geography and IP or device spread on spike days against the merchant's usual customer footprint.
Check the device and terminal telemetry, including any fault logs, restarts or configuration changes around the start of the spike.
Check connectivity and uptime records for the merchant's terminals, to rule out a backlog of offline transactions being pushed through in one batch.
Check whether any settlement or capture failure earlier in the period caused delayed transactions to land together and create an artificial spike.
Pull the chargeback, dispute and refund history for the whole 8 months, and specifically for the spike days, since a genuine sales surge and a fraud burst behave very differently here.
Check authorisation decline rates and failed attempt patterns on the spike days, since heavy card testing shows up as a wall of declines.
Check the issuer-side fraud reports or network alerts, if any, tied to cards transacting on this account.
Pull the settlement history and confirm whether beneficiary bank account details were changed at any point close to the spike.
Review the onboarding file already on record: KYC documents, CIN, PAN, GST details, declared business model, expected monthly turnover and average ticket size.
Compare the actual spike volume against the turnover the merchant declared at onboarding, to see how far outside the declared range it really sits.
Check whether the transaction descriptors, product categories or item details still match MCC 5399, or drift towards a different and higher-risk category.

Check all other merchant IDs, terminals and accounts linked to the same entity, directors, PAN, GST, bank account, email, phone or device, and see whether volume simply moved from one of them to this one.
Check whether any linked account has an existing risk decision, hold or termination against it.
Pull any earlier risk reviews, alerts or holds on this same account, along with what evidence was submitted then and what was concluded.
Check the merchant's API and integration logs for any new plugin, platform or aggregator route switched on just before the spike.
Check whether the spike period overlaps a festival, sale event or seasonal peak that lifted comparable MCC 5399 merchants on the platform, using portfolio-level data.
Check whether the spike has continued, flattened or stopped since the hold was placed, as the shape after day four is itself evidence.

Only if internal records show a new sales channel, platform or integration appearing just before the spike: confirmation of what that channel is and who operates it, to rule out the account being used to process another party's transactions.

Only if the transaction data shows large-ticket or concentrated payments from a few payers: identification of those counterparties and the nature of the dealing, to rule out related-party or circular fund movement.

Only if descriptors, item details or ticket sizes suggest activity outside general merchandise: a current description of goods sold, to test whether the business has drifted away from MCC 5399 and needs recategorisation rather than a fraud hold.
Only if internal records show the settlement bank account was changed near the spike: confirmation of the change from an authorised signatory, to rule out account takeover.

Pull the full 14-month transaction history for this merchant and build the actual ticket size distribution — average value, median, spread, and how many payments fall in each price band — so the "inconsistent ticket size" trigger can be checked against real numbers instead of a summary alert.

Plot the ticket size distribution month by month to see whether the pattern shifted at a specific point in time, which would separate "wrong MCC from day one" from "business changed recently" from "one-off spike".
Extract the exact descriptor text that triggered the flag, including the current descriptor, every past version of it, the date each change was made, and who or what system made the change.

Check whether the descriptor was set by the merchant during onboarding, edited later by the merchant, or auto-generated or altered by an internal tool, bank, or integration partner — a system-generated mismatch is not merchant misconduct.

Re-read the KYC and registration documents already on file (proprietorship registration, GST details, shop licence, bank account name, any trade name) and check whether the business name and stated line of business match sporting goods or point to something else.
Check the merchant's own website, app, or payment page URL as captured at onboarding and any stored screenshots, to see what goods are actually being sold.
Look at the chargeback, refund, and dispute record for the 14 months — a genuine category mismatch that harms customers usually shows up as disputes, while a paperwork mismatch usually does not.
Review customer complaint content in any disputes raised, since complaint text often names the actual product bought and directly confirms or rules out the sporting goods category.
Check the payment method mix, card-present versus online split, and transaction timing pattern against what is typical for sporting goods retail.
Check the refund rate, failed transaction rate, and any unusual same-card or same-customer repeat patterns that would suggest something other than ordinary retail sales.

List every other merchant account, terminal, sub-merchant ID, or payment link held by the same proprietor, same PAN, same bank account, or same registered address, and check whether one of those accounts carries the MCC that actually matches this activity — the merchant may simply be routing sales through the wrong account.
Check whether any of those linked accounts has an open or past risk flag, and whether an earlier risk review already examined this same descriptor or ticket size question and cleared it.

Read all support tickets raised by the merchant across the 14 months, especially any where the merchant mentioned adding new products, changing what they sell, or asked how to update their descriptor or category.
Check whether the aggregator ever sent this merchant a category-change or descriptor-correction notice before, and whether the merchant responded.
Review settlement history and bank credit records to confirm settlements were flowing normally before the hold and that the counterparty bank account has not changed.

Check the merchant's device, terminal, or integration records — which POS terminals or API keys are active, where they are installed, and whether transaction volume is coming from a location or device that does not match the registered shop.

Check billing, rental, and device fault or connectivity logs for the terminals, to rule out the possibility that a shared, relocated, or faulty terminal is producing transactions that are not really this merchant's.

Confirm whether the transaction pattern matches any prohibited or restricted category the aggregator specifically watches for, or only an adjacent permitted retail category — this decides whether the outcome is a simple MCC correction or a serious compliance action.
Record the internal risk rules or model that fired, their thresholds, and the exact data points that breached them, so the file shows what a satisfactory answer would look like.

A plain description from the merchant of what they actually sell today, with a rough breakdown of sales by product type — this is the only way to test the hypothesis that the business genuinely changed or expanded after onboarding, which no internal record can confirm on its own.

Sample sales invoices or bills covering the specific months and the specific ticket sizes that breached the threshold — needed only for those flagged bands, and only to the extent internal checks in items 1 to 3 could not already explain them; this tests whether the unusual amounts are ordinary bulk or high-value sporting goods sales or something outside the category.
Only if internal records show the descriptor was changed by the merchant rather than by a system: an explanation of why the descriptor wording was set that way and what it refers to.

Only if internal device and location records show transactions from a place or terminal not on file: confirmation of the current business address and the list of locations where their terminals are in use.
Full chargeback record for the last 22 months, broken down by month, so we can see whether 2.1% is a sudden spike or a slow climb.

Reason-code split of every chargeback (fraud/unauthorised, item not received, item not as described, duplicate charge, cancelled recurring) — this single split separates a fraud problem from a delivery problem from a quality problem.
Chargeback rate calculated both ways: by count and by value, and against the same month's sales rather than the current month's, to confirm the 2.1% is not just an artefact of falling sales volume.
Whether the 2.1% is concentrated in a few days, a few card BINs, a few issuing banks, or a few end-customers, or spread evenly across the book.
Refund and cancellation rate over the same period — a low refund rate beside a high chargeback rate suggests customers cannot reach the merchant, which is a service problem, not a fraud problem.
Average ticket size trend, and whether disputed transactions sit far above the merchant's normal ticket size.
Mix of card-present versus card-not-present, and domestic versus international cards, in both total sales and disputed sales.
Authentication data on the disputed transactions: 3DS/OTP completion, AVS/CVV outcomes, and whether liability had shifted to the issuer.
Whether disputed transactions were represented (defended) by us or by the merchant, and the win/loss outcome of those representments.
Velocity patterns on the account: sudden surges in transaction count, repeated card numbers, repeated IPs, repeated device fingerprints, unusual hours.

Whether declared MCC 5651 matches observed behaviour — descriptor used, product pages, average ticket, refund pattern — to test the hypothesis of miscoding or transaction laundering for a higher-risk business.

The exact billing descriptor shown on customer statements, and whether it is recognisable as the merchant's brand; an unrecognisable descriptor alone can drive "I don't recognise this charge" chargebacks.
Any customer complaints, issuer retrieval requests, or pre-arbitration notices we already hold, including their text.
Support tickets raised by or about this merchant: delivery complaints, refund delays, failed settlement reports, integration errors.
Payment gateway and API error logs, checkout failure rates, and duplicate-charge or double-submit incidents on our side that could have generated genuine duplicate-transaction disputes.
Any outage, timeout, or reconciliation incident on our platform during the spike window that could have caused failed-but-charged transactions.
Terminal, POS device, and payment-link inventory linked to the merchant, with fault logs, connectivity records, and offline-mode transaction counts if any device is deployed.
Rental, billing, and equipment status for those devices — including any device reported lost, returned, or transferred but still transacting.
All other merchant IDs, terminals, sub-merchants, or accounts tied to the same PAN, GSTIN, CIN, directors, bank account, phone, email, or address, and their dispute rates.
Settlement history: bank account changes, sudden changes in settlement frequency, and any recent request to alter payout details.
Onboarding file and KYC already collected at signup — CIN, PAN, GST, board resolution, director KYC, bank proof, website URL — plus the date it was last refreshed.
Prior risk decisions, earlier reviews, past holds or warnings on this merchant, and what evidence they already submitted then, so we do not ask twice for the same document.
Whether the merchant was already notified of rising disputes before this hold, and how they responded.
Category median methodology check: confirm the 0.4% benchmark is drawn from comparable MCC 5651 merchants of similar size and channel mix, not the whole portfolio.
Current exposure calculation: value on hold, unshipped-order liability estimate, and rolling reserve already held, so the hold size can be justified and sized proportionately.

Evidence of a business change during the spike window — new product line, new courier partner, new marketing channel, flash sale, or a shift to pre-orders and long dispatch times — requested only if item 1 shows a sharp break rather than a gradual rise.

Their current refund and returns policy as published to customers, plus how refund requests reach them, but only if item 5 shows chargebacks far outrunning refunds, suggesting customers could not get a refund the normal way.

Confirmation of who else has access to their payment credentials, keys, or device, requested only if item 10 or item 19 shows patterns consistent with account takeover or an unauthorised reseller using their MID.
Pull the exact account holder name as printed on the bank proof already submitted (cancelled cheque, bank statement, or bank letter) and record it the same way.

Compare the two names after normalising for the differences banks commonly introduce on their own: abbreviation of the suffix, dropped or added full stops, extra or missing spaces, letter case, and truncation caused by bank field length limits. A difference that is fully explained by any of these is a formatting mismatch, not an identity mismatch, and needs nothing from the merchant.

Check the bank account number and IFSC on the bank proof against the settlement account number and IFSC the merchant entered in the onboarding form, and confirm they are identical. A mismatch in the account itself is a different and more serious issue than a name spelling difference.

Check the result of any penny-drop or bank account validation already run on this account. The name returned by the beneficiary name lookup is an independent read of the true account holder name and often settles the question outright.

Check whether this merchant, this CIN, this PAN, or this bank account appears on any other account, terminal, or application in your systems, including rejected or abandoned applications, and pull the KYC decisions and name variants recorded there.

Check the support tickets, emails, and document upload history on this application for earlier versions of the bank proof, for notes from the onboarding team, and for anything the merchant has already explained about the name.

Confirm there is no transaction, settlement, device, connectivity, or rental history to review, since the account has zero months active and has never been activated — record this explicitly so no one re-opens those checks later.

Confirm the flag as raised concerns only the name field, and that the bank proof is otherwise acceptable in type, legibility, and recency under your KYC policy, so that any request to the merchant is limited to the one unresolved point.

Only if checks 3, 4, 6, and 8 leave a real difference in the name — that is, the difference is not explained by abbreviation, formatting, truncation, or a recorded MCA name change, and no penny-drop name is available — ask the merchant for a bank-issued document that carries the full legal entity name: a bank account statement on bank letterhead, a bank confirmation letter, or a passbook first page, showing the same account number and IFSC already on file. Hypothesis this rules out: that the settlement account belongs to a different legal person (a director personally, a sister concern, a predecessor firm, or a trade name) rather than to the incorporated company.

Only if check 6 shows no name change on the MCA record but the bank proof still carries a clearly different company name, ask the merchant for the certified copy of the MCA name-change certificate (Form INC-25 / fresh certificate of incorporation on change of name) or, if the account was opened under a converted proprietorship or partnership, the bank's letter recording the account transfer to the company. Hypothesis this rules out: that the account was opened under an earlier legal name and never updated with the bank, which is benign, as against the account belonging to a separate entity, which is not.

Only if check 5 shows the merchant's declared business name and the certificate of incorporation name differ, ask the merchant to state in writing which name is the legal name and which is the trade or brand name. Hypothesis this rules out: that the mismatch stems from the merchant using a brand name in the settlement account rather than from any change of entity.

Full transaction history on this TID for all 31 months, to see if card activity stopped suddenly (points to a device problem) or faded slowly (points to the business slowing down or switching payment methods).
Activity on all other TIDs, QR codes, UPI handles, or online payment accounts held by the same merchant, to see if the business is still alive but taking payments through another channel.
SIM or network line status for the terminal, to check if the connection was cut off or expired.
Asset and inventory records for this terminal, to check if it was already returned, replaced, swapped, or marked for pickup.
Settlement account history before the gap began, to check for failed payouts or a closed bank account that may have made the merchant stop using the terminal.
Chargeback and dispute history, to rule out that card acceptance stopped after a fraud or dispute problem.
Earlier risk flags or dormancy reviews on this merchant and how they were closed, so past decisions are not repeated or contradicted.
Current KYC file status, to confirm the merchant's details are up to date and no separate re-verification is pending that could be handled in the same pass.

A simple confirmation from the merchant on whether the restaurant is still open and whether they want to keep and use this terminal — only needed if internal checks show the device was healthy, no other payment channel of theirs is active, and no ticket explains the silence. This settles the one question records cannot answer: whether the business has closed, moved to cash or another provider, or plans to resume.

The physical condition and location of the terminal (working, damaged, lost, or in storage) — only needed if telemetry shows the device has been fully offline and there is no support ticket, since an offline device leaves no internal trace of its physical state.

One simple proof that the restaurant is still running, such as a recent utility bill or a current food licence — only needed if the merchant says the business is open but every internal signal (device, other channels, billing) shows no life, to rule out the possibility that the outlet has actually shut down.

Pull the original onboarding file and read the exact partnership legal name recorded there, including spelling, punctuation and any short form used, so the true reference name is fixed before anything is compared.
Pull the current settlement beneficiary record — account number, IFSC, account holder name as held in our system — and note exactly which characters differ from the legal entity name.

Check the penny-drop or account validation response captured when this bank account was first added, since the bank-returned name in that response is the authoritative account holder name and may differ from what was typed in by hand.

Check whether the mismatch is only a formatting or truncation difference — missing "M/s", a dropped suffix, a name cut short by a bank field length limit, extra spaces, or trade name used in place of legal name — because a cosmetic difference is a data issue, not a beneficiary risk issue.

Check the change history on the beneficiary account: when the account was added or last edited, whether the current details are the same ones used at onboarding, and whether any edit happened recently.

If the account was changed, check which user or channel made the change, the IP or device used, and whether it matches the devices and logins normally used by this merchant, since an unfamiliar change source points to account takeover rather than a paperwork error.

Check whether settlements were already paid out to this same account in earlier cycles without a flag, which tells us whether the name mismatch is newly introduced or was present all along and only now detected.

Compare the beneficiary bank account number against the cancelled cheque or bank proof already submitted during onboarding and held on file, since that document may already carry the account holder name we are asking about.
Pull the partnership deed, PAN and GST records already collected at onboarding, and check whether the beneficiary name matches any partner name, the firm's PAN name, or the GST registered name.
Check whether the beneficiary account name matches a partner of the firm, because a partner's personal account is a different situation from a wholly unrelated third party account.
Check all other merchant accounts, terminals and MIDs linked to the same PAN, GST, partners, email, phone or bank account, and see whether the same beneficiary account appears elsewhere in our book.
Check whether that beneficiary account, or the name on it, appears on any internal blocklist, past fraud case, chargeback recovery case, or negative list.
Pull any earlier risk decisions, KYC re-verification notes or past holds on this merchant, so we do not re-litigate a question already answered and closed.

Pull open and past support tickets, emails or calls from this merchant about bank account updates, failed settlements or bank changes, since the merchant may have already explained and documented the change.

Review six months of transaction and settlement history for this merchant — volume, ticket size, refund and chargeback rate, card-present versus online mix — to confirm whether the underlying business behaviour is normal for MCC 5045 or whether the beneficiary change sits alongside other unusual activity.
Check terminal, device and connectivity logs for the period around the beneficiary change, to see whether the merchant's usual terminals were operating normally at that time.
Check billing, rental and invoice records to confirm the account we debit charges from and whether it agrees or disagrees with the settlement beneficiary account.

Only if internal records show the beneficiary name is a genuine third party — not the firm, not a partner, not a formatting variation — ask the merchant to state in writing who owns that account and why settlements are being directed to it, since this is the one fact no internal record can supply and it separates an innocent explanation from proceeds being routed away from the entity.

Only if no bank proof for the current beneficiary account exists on file, or the account was changed after onboarding, ask for a cancelled cheque or bank statement header for that account showing the account holder name, to test whether the account genuinely belongs to the partnership and the mismatch is only in our own data entry.

Only if internal records show the firm's constitution or name appears to have changed — a partner added or removed, a name amended, a conversion of the firm — ask for the updated partnership deed or amended registration, to test the hypothesis that the beneficiary name is correct and our recorded legal entity name is the stale one.

Only if change-history logs show the beneficiary edit came from an unfamiliar user, device or IP, ask the merchant to confirm directly through a verified contact channel that they authorised the change, to rule out account takeover.

Pull the exact address string captured at onboarding, including house/shop number, floor, street, landmark, area, city, state and PIN code, and check whether any of these fields are blank, truncated or clearly mistyped.
Compare the agent's GPS location against the onboarding coordinates and PIN code to see whether the agent went to the correct locality at all.
Check how many visit attempts were made, and whether the single visit fell outside normal working hours, on a Sunday, or on a public holiday.
Check whether the agent tried to phone the merchant during the visit, and whether that call was answered, unanswered or the number was unreachable.
Check the PIN code and locality against a postal or address database to see whether the area itself is one with unnumbered or informal addressing, where "untraceable" is a normal outcome.
Compare the address written on those onboarding proofs word for word against the address stored in the system, to see whether a data entry error created a wrong address in the records.
Retrieve the PAN and the proprietor's KYC record and check the address printed there.
Retrieve the GST registration details on file, if GST was collected, and check the principal place of business address recorded there.
Retrieve the bank account verification record (penny drop or cancelled cheque) and any bank statement already held, and check the address shown on it.

Check whether a welcome kit, POS device, card reader, QR standee or any physical item was ever couriered to the registered address, and pull the courier's delivery confirmation and delivery signature.
Check the asset register for any terminal or device assigned to this merchant, its recorded installation address, and its rental or billing history.
Pull connectivity and fault logs for any assigned device, including the network location and cell or IP data from which it last transacted.
Pull dashboard login logs for the three months of activity: IP addresses, device fingerprints and the approximate locations they map to, and check whether they cluster near the declared address.
Pull the full transaction history for the three months: volume, ticket sizes, timing patterns, and whether the pattern fits an advertising services business or looks unrelated to the declared MCC.
Pull the chargeback, refund, dispute and customer complaint record for the account, since a clean record makes a shell or fake merchant far less likely.
Pull the settlement history and confirm how many settlements were already paid out successfully to the same bank account before this hold.
Pull all support tickets, emails and chat records to see whether the merchant already reported a shift of premises, a correction to the address, or a wrong address in the system.
Check whether any earlier address verification, physical visit or risk review was completed on this merchant and what its outcome was.
Check whether the same PAN, phone number, email address or bank account is linked to any other merchant account or terminal on the platform, and what address those accounts carry.
Check whether any other merchant on the platform is registered at the same address, and whether that address has any past negative history.
Run the merchant, proprietor and address against internal negative lists, dedupe lists and any prior fraud markers.

Confirm whether the registered phone number and email are still live and verified through recent OTP or communication logs, since a contactable merchant points to a bad address record rather than a vanished business.

Only if the internal records show the stored address is incomplete, mistyped, or in an area with informal addressing: a nearby landmark and simple directions to the premises, so a fresh visit can be routed correctly. This tests the hypothesis that the business exists but the written address is not findable on the ground.

Only if the internal records show no usable address proof on file, or show that the proof on file carries a different address from the one in the system: one current address proof in the proprietor's or firm's name, such as a utility bill, rent agreement or Shop and Establishment licence. This tests the hypothesis that the merchant never had a valid address record to begin with.

Only if the bank, GST, KYC or website addresses in the internal records point to a different location than the one visited: written confirmation of the current working address and the date the merchant moved. This tests the hypothesis that the merchant relocated and did not update the records.
